questions.question: What Linux scheduler uses red-black trees for O(log n) complexity?
questions.explanation: CFS maintains processes in a red-black tree ordered by virtual runtime. It ensures fair CPU distribution with excellent scalability.

questions.question: What protocol prevents priority inversion by raising lock holder priority?
questions.explanation: Priority inheritance temporarily elevates the priority of processes holding resources needed by higher-priority processes. This prevents indefinite blocking.

questions.question: What protocol sets resource holder priority to highest waiting process?
questions.explanation: Priority ceiling assigns resources a ceiling priority equal to the highest priority of processes that may use it. This prevents priority inversion proactively.

questions.question: What real-time algorithm schedules based on absolute deadlines?
questions.explanation: EDF is optimal for single-processor real-time scheduling. It selects the process with the nearest absolute deadline to execute next.

questions.question: What algorithm schedules based on rate or period of tasks?
questions.explanation: Rate Monotonic assigns priorities based on task periods. Shorter-period tasks get higher priority in this fixed-priority algorithm.

questions.question: What Linux scheduling class handles real-time processes?
questions.explanation: SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR are real-time scheduling policies in Linux. FIFO runs until blocked while RR uses time slicing.

questions.question: What multiprocessor scheduling assigns processes to specific CPUs?
questions.explanation: Processor affinity binds processes to specific CPUs to maximize cache locality. This reduces cache misses and improves performance.

questions.question: What allows idle CPUs to take processes from busy CPUs?
questions.explanation: Load balancing distributes processes across CPUs to maximize utilization. It can be push migration, pull migration, or both.

questions.question: What Linux nice value provides the highest user-space priority?
questions.explanation: Nice values range from -20 to +19, with lower values meaning higher priority. Only privileged users can set negative nice values.

questions.question: What scheduling favors processes that relinquish CPU voluntarily?
questions.explanation: MLFQ rewards I/O-bound processes by keeping them at higher priority levels. CPU-bound processes gradually move to lower priorities.

questions.question: P1 arrives at 0 (burst 8), P2 at 1 (burst 4), P3 at 2 (burst 9), and P4 at 3 (burst 5). What is the average waiting time under preemptive SJF?
questions.explanation: SRTF runs P1, P2, P4, P1, P3, giving waits of 9, 0, 15, and 2. The average is 26/4 = 6.5 ms.

questions.question: Using the same arrivals (P1 at 0 burst 8, P2 at 1 burst 4, P3 at 2 burst 9, P4 at 3 burst 5), what is the average waiting time under non-preemptive SJF?
questions.explanation: Non-preemptive SJF runs P1, P2, P4, P3 with waits of 0, 7, 15, and 9. The average is 31/4 = 7.75 ms.

questions.question: P1 (burst 8), P2 (burst 4), and P3 (burst 6) all arrive at time 0. With Round Robin and quantum 4, what is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: RR executes P1, P2, P3, P1, P3 with completions at 16, 8, and 18. Waiting times are 8, 4, and 12, averaging 8 ms.

questions.question: With exponential averaging (alpha = 0.5), a last actual burst of 10, and a previous prediction of 12, what is the next predicted burst?
questions.explanation: τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1−α)·τ(n) = 0.5(10) + 0.5(12) = 11. Equal weighting simply averages the last burst and old prediction.

questions.question: As the number of tasks approaches infinity, what value does the rate-monotonic utilization bound approach?
questions.explanation: The RM bound n(2^(1/n) − 1) approaches ln 2 ≈ 0.693. Utilization below about 69% guarantees schedulability for large task sets.
